El Palo Alto. Roughly 1,085 rings.

The handles on the trunk cut a ring around it. Cut anywhere. Everything above the cut dies. That is the whole argument.

The work goes beyond the building.

Declared dying in the late 1920s. Locomotive soot in the crown, wells lowering the water underground. The town piped fog to the top, and it kept growing.

It is still adding rings. The museum opens September 26.

About this drawing

The opening scene is the actual photograph, not a redrawn version of it. It is desaturated and left otherwise alone. The climb above it is drawn, not photographed: an irregular ink line traced through a light turbulence, so the trunk, bark, limbs and roots read as observed rather than generated. Annotations, ticks and the cut handles are left clean on purpose, so the record and the drawing stay visibly two different kinds of mark.

ink
paper
3DAE49

Charcoal and paper carry the record. Green is the only color, and it means one thing: life, flow, and what is still growing. It appears twice, in the sap line that tracks your position up the trunk and stops at any cut, and in the new growth at the crown. Nothing else on the page is green, which is why the bird is drawn in ink.

The bird is notional, drawn after a chestnut-backed chickadee, a small resident of redwood canopy on the Peninsula. It lands on whichever living limb is nearest you, so it climbs as you climb. It will not perch above a cut. Make one low on the trunk and it comes down to the wood that is still carrying water.

Ring count, the moribund declaration, the soot, the wells, the 1955 borings and the fog line follow the Sixteen Conversations surface note. The brand language is verbatim from the August 2026 one-pager, with one adaptation: "Everything below the lens follows from the lens" became "Everything above it rises through it," because this drawing reads upward instead of downward. Fact and drawing are labeled apart; where the drawing invents, it says so here.
